preview: Kalp Mehta shares his Mahindra Finance summer internship interview experience, detailing the online aptitude test, coding assessment, technical interview, and HR round.
content: Kalp Mehta Mahindra Finance Internship Experience. The Mahindra Finance Summer Internship process began with an initial resume shortlisting round, followed by two rounds — an aptitude test and a coding assessment. OA: Round 1 – Aptitude Test (25/11/25) The test included questions from: General English – mainly comprehension and grammar Quantitative Aptitude – basic arithmetic, percentages, and logical reasoning Analytical Thinking Overall, the difficulty level was easy. The focus was more on speed and accuracy rather than advanced concepts. Round 2 – Coding Assessment (26/11/25) Candidates who cleared the aptitude round were shortlisted for the online coding assessment, conducted the very next day. This round had two sections: 1. Python MCQs (20 questions, 15–20 minutes) – Covering topics like loops, functions, data types, and error handling. 2. Coding Problems (3 questions) – Only Python was allowed. The coding problems were simple and logic-based. I was able to solve all three within the given time and ensured that my code was clean and readable. Pre-Interview Session (PPT) (28/11/25) On 28th November, Mahindra Finance conducted an offline PPT on campus. I would strongly recommend attending this session seriously, as it gives you a clear understanding of: The company’s core operations and values The kind of skills and mindset they expect from interns It’s also a very good opportunity to ask thoughtful and relevant questions. One thing I personally noticed was that the students who showed genuine interest and asked good questions were being observed. Since this was our first PPT for Mahindra Finance, we weren’t fully aware of how important that could be for us. Interview Day – 29th November 2025 The interviews were scheduled offline, and candidates were given the option to choose between two roles one day prior: IT Role Data Analyst Role I chose the IT role. Out of 20 shortlisted candidates, 8 opted for IT and 12 for Data Analyst. Round 1 – Technical Interview My technical interview was scheduled 5th in order started around 11:45 am and lasted around 35–40 minutes. The interviewer began by asking for a brief introduction. I gave a short and structured overview mentioning my branch, minor, key interests, and 1–2 important projects I had worked on. I would suggest not memorizing a fixed introduction. Instead, be clear about what you want to include and present it naturally. This introduction actually set the tone for the rest of the interview. Since I mentioned projects like QRLY and NEP Timetable Generator, she asked me to explain one of them in depth starting from the idea behind it to how I implemented it. We discussed why I chose specific tech stacks and how I integrated the different components. I realized they were not just evaluating technical skills, but also how clearly I could think and communicate my approach. One important thing know your projects inside out. Be clear about: The real-world problem it solves The use case Why you chose a particular approach How it connects to the job description For example, the job role involved data collection and analysis, and my QRLY project aligned well with that. That alignment definitely worked in my favor. After the project discussion, she moved to SQL. I was asked to write and explain queries such as: Create, Alter, delete, and replace queries Difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE Finding the 3rd highest salary from an employee table (in two different ways) I explained both the syntax and the reasoning behind each query. It’s important to understand that they are not just testing memorization they want to see whether you truly understand what each command does. For example, I didn’t remember the exact syntax of the ALTER command , but my concept was clear and I was close to the solution. That clarity matters more than word-to-word accuracy. Next, she asked a conceptual question from Operating Systems about Multithreading. I explained how multiple threads run concurrently to improve performance, and briefly discussed synchronization and some scheduling concepts. We discussed working of different scheduling algorithms also mentioned one of the algorithms which I have used in my one of the project at backend for load balancing. How it works practically and etc. Then came a situation-based question aligned with the IT role. She presented a real-world scenario: “Let’s say the UPI organization introduces new features and functionalities. What measures would you take before integrating them into the Mahindra Finance system?” I approached it step by step first understanding the requirements, then considering security implications, backward compatibility, system impact analysis, testing in a staging environment, and ensuring proper validation before deployment. I tried to structure my answer logically rather than jumping straight to a technical solution. Towards the end, she asked some behavioral and company-related questions, such as: “Why do you want to join Mahindra Finance?” “What interests you about this role?” Since I had paid attention during the PPT and done some research, I connected my answers to their digital initiatives and my interest in working on scalable, data-driven systems. Finally, I asked two thoughtful questions one about Mahindra Finance’s future scope in digitization and another about one related to the recent news of company . She appreciated the curiosity, and we had a meaningful two-way discussion. The interview ended on a very positive note. It felt more like a professional conversation than a strict Q&A session. One key thing to remember: during the interview, stay attentive and try to align yourself with the job description. Understand what problem they are trying to solve and position yourself as someone who can contribute to that solution. Post-Interview Thoughts Walking out of the interview room, I felt satisfied. It wasn’t perfect, but it was genuine — a mix of learning, clarity, and confidence. A few hours later, I received the message that I had been shortlisted for the HR round. Looking back, the key takeaway from this round is simple: “Know your resume deeply, understand your projects inside-out, and express your thoughts clearly. They’re not looking for perfection — they’re looking for potential.” Round 2 – HR Interview After the technical interviews concluded, a total of 8 candidates were shortlisted for the HR round 4 from the IT role and 4 from the DnA (Data & Analytics) role. To be honest, I was slightly more nervous for this round, because I hadn’t had much time to specifically prepare for HR-style questions. Most of my preparation time had gone into technical topics. So instead of overthinking, I decided to just be myself and keep the conversation as natural as possible. And honestly, that approach worked well. Starting the Conversation The HR greeted me warmly and, after a brief exchange of greetings, asked: “Give a brief introduction about yourself from childhood to where you are today.” I took a moment to organize my thoughts and then narrated my journey in a story-like format starting from my early education, how I developed curiosity for technology, and how that gradually led me to pursue Electronics & Telecommunication Engineering at VJTI. I also spoke about how my interest in software development evolved over time and how working on projects and in teams helped me build problem-solving skills and handle deadlines. I ended by mentioning a few hobbies and personal qualities that reflect how I approach work being analytical, consistent, and comfortable in collaborative environments. For this part, just be genuine. And wherever possible, subtly highlight qualities like leadership, adaptability, time management, and teamwork through your journey rather than directly claiming them. The Puzzle Question Next, he gave me a small puzzle question. I hadn’t specifically prepared puzzles, but I tried to think calmly and solve it logically during the conversation. If I could give one suggestion here practice a few common puzzles beforehand from platforms like GeeksforGeeks. They’re usually not very difficult. The goal is to see how you think aloud, structure your reasoning, and stay composed under pressure. Situation-Based and Behavioral Questions After that, the HR moved to a few situation-based questions, which are quite common in HR rounds. For example: “If a teammate suddenly leaves in the middle of a project, how would you handle it?” “If your manager has a different approach to a task than yours, how would you deal with it?” For such questions, I focused on giving balanced and practical answers. I explained that I would first understand the other person’s perspective, communicate my suggestions respectfully, and then align with the final team decision keeping a learning mindset and prioritizing the overall project’s success. For the team scenario, I shared an example from one of my college projects where we managed workload distribution, handled last-minute issues, and maintained coordination even under pressure. The key takeaway here is: Always frame your answers to reflect teamwork, adaptability, ownership, and problem-solving. Avoid rigid responses like “I’ll just follow the manager blindly.” Instead, show that you respect hierarchy but can also think critically and communicate effectively. Questions to the HR (The Most Important Part) Towards the end which I personally feel was the strongest part of the entire interview the HR asked if I had any questions for him. Many candidates underestimate this moment, but it’s actually a great opportunity to leave a lasting impression. Based on my prior research about Mahindra Finance and its initiatives, I asked a couple of thoughtful questions related to their digital transformation journey and how technology is shaping their operations. These weren’t generic questions, but more strategic and forward-looking. He appreciated the depth and mentioned that it reflected genuine interest. I then asked about his personal experience at Mahindra Finance. His answer was very passionate he spoke about the culture, ownership, innovation, and what makes the organization stand out from an employee’s perspective. I wrapped up by connecting his response with my own interest in working at a place that combines technology with meaningful real-world impact, especially at the common man’s level. That made the ending feel very natural and engaging more like a conversation than an interview. The Result On 2nd December 2025,the final results were announced ,and I was selected. Looking back, this achievement was not just mine. It was built on the constant support and encouragement of my seniors, friends, and family. I am truly grateful to everyone who guided and stood by me throughout this journey.
